title: Short Stuff: Color Psychology
summary: Short Stuff episode on color psychology. Josh and Chuck open with banter about color drenching a bedroom and Josh's 1990s burgundy, dark blue and hunter green decor. They explain that color meaning is not universal: it varies by culture, personal experience and mood, and color symbolism (e.g., black for mourning in the West versus white in parts of the East, green for luck traced to Ireland). Chuck cites cross-cultural findings comparing American and Japanese color associations, and wonders about purple at funerals at a local African American church. After a break, they discuss the Crayola eight-pack's main colors: red (strength, courage, heart rate, stop signs), orange (mixed associations), black (power, authority, Western black hats, black hat hackers), and yellow (cowardice, cheerfulness, the unproven 'cry longer in yellow room' idea). They stress shades and light matter, and advise testing paint samples in different lighting.

segments.title: Opening and setup
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as a Short Stuff, with Jerry sitting in for Dave.

segments.title: What color psychology is
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh explain that color reactions depend on culture, upbringing, age, mood and personal experience, so there is no universal meaning. They note that color psychology studies this and that marketers use broad cultural patterns.

segments.title: Color drenching banter
segments.summary: Chuck describes color drenching, painting walls, ceiling, trim and doors one color, and says he and his partner plan a deep green bedroom. Josh recalls 1990s burgundy, dark blue and hunter green decor.

segments.title: Color symbolism and culture
segments.summary: Josh explains that color symbolism is set by culture: black for mourning in the West and white in parts of the East, and green for luck traced to Ireland and leprechauns. Personal experiences, such as a childhood bear encounter, also shape reactions.

segments.title: Cross-cultural color studies and funeral purple
segments.summary: Chuck cites cross-cultural studies comparing American and Japanese associations of warm and cool colors, with blue and green seen as good in Japan and red, purple and orange as bad. He wonders whether purple at funerals at a local African American church reflects a community custom or personal preference.

segments.title: Break transition
segments.summary: Brief transition into a break, with the hosts setting up the Crayola eight-pack discussion.

segments.title: Crayola eight-pack intro and red
segments.summary: The hosts say they will cover highlights of the Crayola eight-pack's main colors. Chuck covers red: associations with boldness, strength, courage and aggression, a possible link to getting pulled over in a red car, heart-rate effects, and use on stop signs and warning labels.

segments.title: Orange and black
segments.summary: Josh says he likes orange but notes many people dislike it and that its associations are mixed. Chuck likes browns, greens and oranges. Chuck then discusses black as powerful and authoritative, shades of black in paint, Western black and white hats, and black hat hackers.

segments.title: Yellow and shades
segments.summary: Josh covers yellow: its link to cowardice in older usage, its cheerfulness, and the unproven claim that people cry longer in yellow rooms. He stresses that saturation, value and hue change how a color feels, so pale yellow and neon yellow have different effects.

segments.title: Paint testing advice and sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck advises testing small paint samples on the wall and viewing them in different light, since daylight changes hue. Josh jokes about flashlights, and they sign off.
